DifferentialGamesBenchmarks.jl

DifferentialGamesBenchmarks.jl provides benchmark cases, assumption-removal challenges, independent evaluation metrics, experiment orchestration and Makie-based visualization for the ecosystem. A benchmark case always builds a real Base game, never a private copy, so anything that solves a Base game can be benchmarked.

Its role in the ecosystem is evaluation: it consumes games (Base) and solutions produced by any solver that follows the solver contract (Solvers, or your own package), and scores them with metrics that do not rely on the solver's own convergence flag.

Status

The examples below were run against the current sources (Julia 1.12) and are not executed during the documentation build. Plotting requires CairoMakie or GLMakie, which are extensions.

Concepts

ConceptMeaning
CaseID(name, variant, version)identity of a case, e.g. SimplePursuit.Nominal_v1
BenchmarkCasean immutable, versioned reference to a case: id, a zero-argument build factory, a default AccessSpec, a description and references; game(case) rebuilds a fresh Base game every call, so cases are reproducible
CASE_REGISTRY, register_case!, lookup_caseregistry of cases; the official ones are registered at load time
AccessSpec (FullModelAccess, ApproximateModelAccess, SimulatorOnlyAccess, ModelFreeAccess, MaskedObjectives, ObservationOnlyAccess)what the solver is allowed to know about the game; the same case can be offered to model-based and learning-based methods
ChallengeProfile and transforms add_process_noise, add_disturbance_bound, restrict_observation, restrict_communicationremove assumptions by wrapping the game in the Base uncertainty types (StochasticGameProblem, RobustGameProblem, POGameProblem, communication limits)
Evaluator, evaluatemetrics recomputed from the trajectories: validity (constraint satisfaction), quality (e.g. cost-consistency residual, capture radius), robustness (dynamics residual), efficiency (solve time and iterations)
Experiment, Benchmark, Budget, run, ExperimentResultorchestration of case × solver × challenge × budget

Official cases

CaseCaseIDWhat it stresses
Simple pursuitSimplePursuit.Nominal_v1minimal single-integrator pursuit–evasion
Homicidal chauffeurHomicidalChauffeur.Nominal_v1dynamics asymmetry: bounded-turning-radius pursuer vs a free evader
Game of two carsGameOfTwoCars.Nominal_v1dynamics symmetry: both players are bounded-turning-radius cars
Lady in the lakeLadyInTheLake.Nominal_v1asymmetric domain: free-swimming evader vs a pursuer confined to a 1-D shore
LQ formationLQFormation.Nominal_v1leader/follower LQ Nash game with a known closed-form solution (the analytic reference backbone)
Hallway passingHallwayPassing.Nominal_v1three unicycles through an S-shaped double-choke corridor, from the FALCON suite (page)
Racing (Austin)Racing.AustinNominal_v1two dynamic-bicycle cars racing head-to-head, from the FALCON suite (page)

The four pursuit–evasion cases are built on the PD-GNEP path and are solved with ALGAMES (the turning-rate bounds of the chauffeur and two-cars cases need constraint support). The LQ case is solved exactly by FNELQ. The hallway and racing cases are hard non-convex problems that no solver here converges on; see the benchmark suite for the full catalogue, including the multi-agent particle tasks of the MADDPG paper.

Example

using DifferentialGamesBenchmarks, DifferentialGamesBase, DifferentialGamesBaseSolvers

case = SIMPLE_PURSUIT_NOMINAL_V1
g    = game(case)                                          # a Base GameProblem
sol  = DifferentialGamesBase.solve(g, ALGAMES())
res  = evaluate(simple_pursuit_evaluator(), g, sol)

res.quality[:time_to_capture]            # 3.3
res.quality[:capture_radius_min]         # 0.42
res.quality[:nash_residual]              # Dict(1 => 0.0, 2 => 0.0): reported vs recomputed cost, see the warning below
res.validity[:constraints_satisfied]

Or through the orchestration layer:

experiment = Experiment(case, ALGAMES(); evaluator = simple_pursuit_evaluator())
result = DifferentialGamesBenchmarks.run(experiment)

Exact solutions give an analytic check of the whole stack: for the LQ formation case

case = LQ_FORMATION_NOMINAL_V1
sol  = DifferentialGamesBase.solve(game(case), FNELQ())
evaluate(lq_formation_evaluator(), game(case), sol).quality[:formation_error_final]   # ≈ 2·10⁻⁶

(Call run as DifferentialGamesBenchmarks.run to avoid ambiguity with Base.run.)

`:nash_residual` is a cost-consistency check

Despite its name, the default quality metric game_quality_nash_residual compares each player's recomputed cost with the cost the solver reported. It catches misreported objectives but does not test optimality: it returned 0 for a racing solution whose own optimality residual was of order 10³. A genuine equilibrium test (a best response against the other players' fixed trajectories) is not yet in the package.

Visualization

With CairoMakie (static) or GLMakie (interactive) loaded: gameplot(case, sol; preset = :publication), dashboard(result), animate, interactive, renderframe. Visual models are registered per case with register_visualizer!.

Relationship to the rest of the ecosystem

  • Base supplies the games, the uncertainty wrappers used by challenges and the solution types read by evaluators.
  • Solvers are used through the DifferentialGamesBenchmarksSolversExt extension; any solver following the solver contract can be benchmarked.
  • MARL: a case's game can be wrapped in a MADDPGEnv and a trained agent evaluated in the same way; the ModelFreeAccess/SimulatorOnlyAccess specifications describe such use.
  • The package also served to find defects in the solvers: while building the LQ formation case an affine-term sign error in FNELQ was identified independently (it is now fixed in the sibling working tree, see the audit).
